unit-1.title: Sounds and Stories
unit-1.description: Phonics: initial sounds, blending, and listening to and retelling simple stories.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 -- Learning Initial Sounds
lessons.objectives: Recognise and say the sounds of the letters s, a, t, p; identify the initial (first) sound in a spoken word.

steps.title: What is an initial sound?
steps.definition: The initial sound is the very first sound you hear at the start of a word.
steps.example: The word "sun" starts with the /s/ sound. The word "ant" starts with the /a/ sound.

cards.label: s
cards.content: Sounds like a snake hissing: /s/. As in "sun".

cards.label: t
cards.content: A quick tap sound: /t/. As in "tree".

cards.label: p
cards.content: A little pop sound: /p/. As in "pineapple".

summaryPoints: The initial sound is the first sound at the start of a word.
We practised the sounds s, a, t, p.
homeworkItems: Find one thing at home that starts with the /s/ sound and tell your family.

teachingScript.overview: Say each sound in isolation (not the letter name) and exaggerate it slightly so children can hear it clearly before matching it to a word.

talkingPoints: Say "sun" slowly, stretching the /s/ so children can hear it separated from the rest of the word.
Have children say each sound aloud with you, not just listen -- repetition builds the sound-symbol link.
Give a physical action for right answers (thumbs up) to keep energy high at this age.
misconceptions: Children may say the letter name ("tee") instead of the sound (/t/) -- gently model the sound each time.

talkingPoints: Go round the circle quickly, each child naming one word starting with today's sounds.

quizQuestions.question: Which word starts with the /s/ sound?
The word "ant" starts with which sound?

flashcards.definition: The first sound you hear at the start of a word.
Sounds like a snake hissing: /s/, as in "sun".
A short sound: /a/, as in "ant".
A quick tap sound: /t/, as in "tree".
A little pop sound: /p/, as in "pineapple".

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Learning Initial Sounds
worksheetContent.instructions: Say each picture's name out loud before you answer.

questions.prompt: Circle the pictures that start with the /s/ sound (e.g. sun, sand, snake).
Draw one thing that starts with the /p/ sound.
Say the word "tap" slowly. What sound does it start with?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 -- Blending Sounds to Read Words
lessons.objectives: Blend two or three letter sounds together smoothly to read a simple word (e.g. s-a-t = sat).

steps.title: What is blending?
steps.definition: Blending means saying each sound separately, then pushing them together smoothly to read the whole word.
steps.example: s...a...t said slowly becomes "sat" when we blend the sounds together quickly.

summaryPoints: Blending means pushing separate sounds together to make a word.
We blended sat, sit, and tap today.
homeworkItems: Practise blending s-u-n with a grown-up.

teachingScript.overview: Use finger-pointing (one finger per sound) to make blending physically visible before children try it alone.

talkingPoints: Physically slide your finger under each sound as you say it, then sweep quickly under the whole word for the blend.
Do this several times at different speeds -- very slow, then a little faster, then blended -- so children hear the transition.
Have children say each answer aloud with you before selecting it, since hearing themselves blend matters more than the answer itself.
misconceptions: Children may guess a similar-looking word instead of actually blending the sounds -- always ask them to say the sounds first.

talkingPoints: Finish with a quick round where each child blends one word aloud.

quizQuestions.question: Blending means...
options: Pushing separate sounds together to make a word

flashcards.definition: Pushing separate sounds together smoothly to read a whole word.
Blended from the sounds /s/-/a/-/t/.
Blended from the sounds /s/-/i/-/t/.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Blending Sounds to Read Words
worksheetContent.instructions: Say each set of sounds slowly, then blend them together.

questions.prompt: Blend s-a-t. What word did you make?
Blend t-a-p. What word did you make?
Draw a picture of one of the words you blended.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 -- Listening to and Retelling a Story
lessons.objectives: Listen attentively to a simple story or nursery rhyme; retell the main events in order (beginning, middle, end) using pictures or simple words.

steps.title: Every story has an order
steps.definition: A story has a beginning (what happens first), a middle (what happens next), and an end (what happens last).
steps.example: In a story about a lost puppy: the beginning is the puppy getting lost, the middle is looking for it, and the end is finding it and going home.

cards.definition: What happens first in the story.
What happens next, after the beginning.
What happens last, to finish the story.

items.label: The puppy gets lost in the market.
items.reason: This is what starts the story and sets up the problem.

items.label: The children search everywhere for the puppy.
items.reason: This is what happens as a result of the beginning, before the problem is solved.

items.label: The puppy is found asleep under a table and everyone goes home happy.
items.reason: This is how the story finishes -- the problem is solved.

summaryPoints: Every story has a beginning, a middle, and an end.
Retelling a story means saying the events in the right order.
homeworkItems: Retell your favourite story to a grown-up, using the words beginning, middle, and end.

teachingScript.overview: Read a real, familiar short story or nursery rhyme aloud first, then map it onto beginning/middle/end together as a class before independent sorting practice.

talkingPoints: Read a short, familiar story aloud in full before naming its beginning/middle/end.
Ask children to point to where in the room "beginning," "middle," and "end" would be if the story were a walk across the room.
Use picture cards from the story just read if you have them, rather than only the puppy example.
misconceptions: Children may retell events in the order they remember them rather than the order they happened -- gently prompt "what happened first?"

talkingPoints: Have one or two volunteers retell the whole story in one sentence each for beginning/middle/end.

quizQuestions.question: The part of the story that happens first is called the...
"The puppy is found and everyone goes home happy" is most likely the...

flashcards.definition: What happens first in a story.
What happens next in a story.
What happens last in a story.
To tell a story again, in your own words, in the right order.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Listening to and Retelling a Story
worksheetContent.instructions: Think about the story we listened to in class.

questions.prompt: Draw what happened at the beginning of the story.
Draw what happened at the end of the story.
Tell a grown-up what happened in the middle.

unit-2.title: Writing Our Ideas
unit-2.description: Pencil grip and letter formation, writing simple words, and writing a simple punctuated sentence.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 -- Holding a Pencil and Forming Letters
lessons.objectives: Hold a pencil correctly using a comfortable, controlled grip; form letters starting and finishing in the right place.

steps.title: A good pencil grip
steps.definition: A good pencil grip means holding the pencil gently between your thumb and first two fingers, not squeezing it tightly in your fist.
steps.example: It's like holding a small twig you don't want to snap -- gentle, but steady enough to control where it goes.

cards.label: Thumb and two fingers
cards.content: Hold the pencil with your thumb and first two fingers, like a tiny tripod.

cards.label: Gentle, not tight
cards.content: Squeezing too hard makes your hand tired and your writing shaky.

cards.label: Steady the paper
cards.content: Use your other hand to hold the paper still while you write.

cards.question: Someone is holding the pencil in their whole fist, squeezing it very tightly. Is this a good grip?
cards.answer: No -- squeezing tightly in a fist makes writing tiring and hard to control.

cards.question: Someone is holding the pencil gently between their thumb and two fingers. Is this a good grip?
cards.answer: Yes! This gentle tripod grip gives the best control.

summaryPoints: A good grip uses the thumb and first two fingers, held gently.
Steady the paper with your other hand.
homeworkItems: Practise holding a pencil correctly while colouring or drawing at home.

teachingScript.overview: Model the grip on your own hand up close, then walk round to check and gently correct each child's grip individually during practice.

talkingPoints: Hold your own pencil up close so children can see the exact finger placement.
Have children practise the grip in the air with an imaginary pencil before picking up a real one.
Demonstrate both a fist-squeeze grip and a correct grip live so the contrast is obvious.
misconceptions: Children who have been colouring with a fist grip may find the tripod grip tiring at first -- reassure them this is normal and improves with practice.

talkingPoints: Give each child one minute of quiet practice while you check grips individually.

quizQuestions.question: A good pencil grip uses...
options: Your thumb and first two fingers

quizQuestions.question: While writing, your other hand should...

flashcards.definition: How you hold a pencil -- gently, with your thumb and first two fingers.
To hold something still, like your paper while writing.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Holding a Pencil and Forming Letters
worksheetContent.instructions: Check your grip before you start each line.

questions.prompt: Trace the dotted lines and circles on this page using your best pencil grip.
Trace the letters s, a, t, p, following the arrows.
Show a grown-up your pencil grip. Did they say it looked steady?

lessons.title: Lesson 5 -- Writing Simple Words
lessons.objectives: Write simple CVC (consonant-vowel-consonant) words independently, such as cat, dog, sun, using known letter sounds.

steps.title: Writing a word sound by sound
steps.definition: Many simple words are made of three sounds: consonant, vowel, consonant (a "CVC" word). We write each sound in order.
steps.example: The word "sun" has three sounds: /s/, /u/, /n/. We write s, then u, then n.

questions.question: How many sounds are in the word "cat"?
What is the middle sound in "dog"?

summaryPoints: We write a word by saying it slowly and writing each sound in order.
We practised writing sun, cat and dog.
homeworkItems: Practise writing one CVC word (e.g. cat, dog, sun) three times at home.

teachingScript.overview: Say the word aloud slowly as a class before anyone writes, so children hear the sounds separated before committing them to paper.

talkingPoints: Clap once per sound as you say "sun" slowly, so the three-sound structure is felt physically.
Write on the board sound by sound, pausing to say each sound again before writing the next letter.
Have children count sounds on their fingers before answering.
misconceptions: Children may confuse letter names and sounds when counting -- keep the focus on the sound, not the letter name.

talkingPoints: Ask a few children to write one CVC word on the board with support.

quizQuestions.question: A CVC word has this pattern of sounds:
Which of these is a CVC word?

flashcards.definition: A word made of three sounds: consonant, vowel, consonant, e.g. cat, sun, dog.
A letter sound that isn't a, e, i, o, or u -- like s, t, p, c, d, n, g.
One of the letter sounds a, e, i, o, u.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Writing Simple Words
worksheetContent.instructions: Say each word slowly before you write it.

questions.prompt: Write the word "cat" sound by sound.
Write the word "sun" sound by sound.
Draw a picture to match one of your words.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 -- Writing a Simple Sentence
lessons.objectives: Write a simple sentence using a capital letter at the start, finger spaces between words, and a full stop at the end.

steps.title: What makes a sentence?
steps.definition: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, with spaces between each word.
steps.example: "The cat sat." starts with a capital T, has a space between each word, and ends with a full stop.

cards.label: Capital letter
cards.content: A big letter at the very start of the sentence.

cards.label: Finger spaces
cards.content: A small gap, about the width of a finger, between each word.

cards.label: Full stop
cards.content: A small dot at the end, to show the sentence has finished.

cards.question: "the cat sat" -- with no capital letter and no full stop. Is this finished correctly?
cards.answer: Not quite! It needs a capital T at the start and a full stop at the end: "The cat sat."

cards.question: "The dog ran." -- with a capital letter and a full stop. Is this finished correctly?
cards.answer: Yes! It has a capital letter, finger spaces, and a full stop.

summaryPoints: A sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.
We leave a finger space between each word.
homeworkItems: Write one sentence at home about your day, remembering the capital letter and full stop.

teachingScript.overview: Write an example sentence on the board with all three features missing first, then fix it together as a class before independent writing.

talkingPoints: Write "the cat sat" with no capital or full stop, and ask what's missing before you explain.
Have children use an actual finger to check spacing on their own first attempt.
Fix the incorrect example together as a class, adding the capital letter and full stop live.
misconceptions: Children often remember the full stop but forget the capital letter, or vice versa -- check for both explicitly.

talkingPoints: Have a few children read their own sentence aloud, pointing to the capital letter and full stop as they go.

quizQuestions.question: A sentence should start with a...
A sentence should end with a...

flashcards.definition: A group of words starting with a capital letter and ending with a full stop.
A big letter used at the start of a sentence.
A small dot used at the end of a sentence.
A small gap, about the width of a finger, left between words.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Writing a Simple Sentence
worksheetContent.instructions: Remember: capital letter, finger spaces, full stop.

questions.prompt: Write a sentence about your favourite animal.
Check your sentence: does it have a capital letter at the start? Circle it.
Check your sentence: does it have a full stop at the end? Circle it.

unit-3.title: Speaking and Listening Together
unit-3.description: Speaking clearly and taking turns; listening carefully and following instructions.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 -- Speaking Clearly and Taking Turns
lessons.objectives: Speak clearly so others can understand; take turns when speaking in a group and wait for others to finish.

steps.title: Taking turns to speak
steps.definition: Taking turns means waiting until someone else has finished speaking before you start, so everyone gets a chance to be heard.
steps.example: In a circle, we might pass a small object around -- only the person holding it speaks, and everyone else listens.

cards.label: Clear voice
cards.content: Speak loud enough for everyone in the circle to hear, but not shouting.

cards.label: Look at your listener
cards.content: Looking at the person you're speaking to helps them know you're talking to them.

cards.label: Wait your turn
cards.content: Let the speaker finish their whole idea before you start talking.

questions.question: Two friends are both talking loudly at the same time. Is this good turn-taking?
options: No -- only one person should speak at a time
questions.feedback: ✓ Talking over each other means no one can be properly heard.

questions.question: A friend waits until you finish your sentence, then speaks. Is this good turn-taking?
questions.feedback: ✓ Waiting for a turn lets everyone be heard clearly.

summaryPoints: Speak clearly and look at your listener.
Wait your turn so everyone gets to be heard.
homeworkItems: Practise taking turns to talk during dinner at home tonight.

teachingScript.overview: Use a real object (a small ball or soft toy) as a physical "talking piece" during circle time to make turn-taking concrete for this age group.

talkingPoints: Introduce the talking-piece object and explain the rule: only the holder speaks.
Model a too-quiet voice and a good clear voice so children hear the contrast.
Role-play both the interrupting example and the good example live before asking the question.
Run one full round of the circle using the talking piece so every child gets a turn to practise.
misconceptions: Some children may want to speak again out of turn -- gently remind them the object shows whose turn it is.

quizQuestions.question: Taking turns means...
options: Waiting until someone finishes before you speak

quizQuestions.question: When you speak, it helps to...
options: Look at your listener and speak clearly

flashcards.definition: Waiting until someone else finishes speaking before you start.
A voice loud enough for your listener to hear, but not shouting.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Speaking Clearly and Taking Turns
worksheetContent.instructions: Think about our circle time talking practice.

questions.prompt: Draw a picture of you speaking to a friend and looking at them.
Tell a grown-up one thing you remember about taking turns.
Practise waiting for a grown-up to finish talking before you speak, at home tonight.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 -- Listening Carefully and Following Instructions
lessons.objectives: Listen carefully to spoken instructions and follow them in the correct order, including instructions with two or more steps.

steps.title: Following instructions in order
steps.definition: An instruction tells us what to do. Some instructions have more than one step, and we need to remember the order.
steps.example: "Stand up, then touch your toes" has two steps -- first stand up, then touch your toes, in that order.

steps.label: Listen to the whole instruction first

questions.question: The instruction is: "Pick up your pencil, then write your name." What should you do first?
questions.feedback: ✓ The instruction says pick up your pencil first, then write your name.

questions.question: The instruction is: "Stand up, turn around, sit back down." How many steps are there?
questions.feedback: ✓ Stand up, turn around, and sit back down -- three steps in order.

summaryPoints: Listen to the whole instruction before starting.
Remember the order: what comes first, then next.
homeworkItems: Ask a grown-up to give you a two-step instruction at home and follow it in order.

teachingScript.overview: Play a short physical "Simon Says"-style game with two-step instructions to make listening-and-following an active, memorable practice, not just a talking point.

talkingPoints: Give one very simple one-step instruction first ("stand up") so the concept is anchored before adding a second step.
Physically demonstrate the two-step instruction yourself before asking children to try it.
Ask children to repeat the instruction back in their own words before answering, to check they really listened.
misconceptions: Children may do the steps in the wrong order, or skip the first step -- praise attempts and gently replay the instruction if needed.

talkingPoints: Play a quick round of two-step "Simon says" instructions as a fun, physical recap.

quizQuestions.question: Before following an instruction, you should...
options: Listen to the whole instruction first
Ask someone else to do it

quizQuestions.question: "Touch your head, then touch your toes" -- what should you do second?

flashcards.definition: Words that tell us what to do.
Doing things in the correct sequence -- first, then next.

worksheetContent.title: Worksheet -- Listening Carefully and Following Instructions
worksheetContent.instructions: A grown-up will read each instruction aloud to you.

questions.prompt: Listen to a two-step instruction from a grown-up, then draw yourself doing step one.
Draw yourself doing step two of the same instruction.
Tell a grown-up which step came first.
